sections.title: Four-part notation
sections.text: Tempo is often written as four numbers: the lowering phase, the pause at the bottom, the lifting phase and the pause at the top. In a squat, 3-1-1-0 means lower for three seconds, pause one second at the bottom, rise in one second, and start the next rep right away. Not every system lists the phases in the same order, so the instructions have to say which notation they use.

sections.title: Why control helps
sections.text: A slow lowering phase can stop you bouncing, show up balance problems, and make light loads hard enough for skill practice. A short pause can help you feel your position at a sticking point. Lifting fast on purpose may help strength or power work when your technique is safe and the load suits it.

sections.title: Tempo and hypertrophy
sections.text: Research has not shown that very slow reps reliably produce more growth. The 2026 ACSM position stand found that time under tension was not a consistent factor when different training plans were compared. Going extremely slow can cut the load or total reps you manage and may work against your main goal.

sections.title: Example
sections.text: If you are learning a hinge, lowering a dumbbell over two to three seconds gives you time to keep the weight close and feel your hips move back. Once the pattern is consistent, a normal controlled speed may be enough. A medicine-ball throw or a jump is meant to be fast, so don’t slow it down.

sections.title: Comparing sets
sections.text: When you judge progress, compare sets done with a similar range and speed. Adding weight while cutting the lowering phase short may not be a real improvement. Unless a skill calls for a set tempo, focus on steady, controlled reps and your main goal, and don’t count every second.
